title: Teaching on Purpose #5: Live Modelling
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Kohlbeck's fifth installment in the Teaching on Purpose series focuses on live modelling as a technique for communicating meaning in the classroom, based on an interview with Noureddine Mlaouhi, Assistant Headteacher at Putteridge High School. The series is organized around six core teaching purposes at Chiltern Learning Trust: securing attention, communicating meaning, driving student thinking, providing and scaffolding practice, utilizing memory, and checking for understanding. Live modelling—building up a model piece by piece in real time while narrating the thought process—is presented through three decision-making scenarios: when to use it as-designed, when to adapt it, and when to skip it entirely. The article argues that mid-model checks for understanding are not interruptions but diagnostic moments that reveal whether prior knowledge required for the model to work is actually secure; when it is not, the teacher must step away, re-teach the required knowledge, and then return to the model. When students already have secure knowledge of both content and process, withholding the model until after independent work allows the gap between their attempt and the ideal to generate its own learning. Kohlbeck uses the example of annotating a quotation in Year 10 English to make the three decision points concrete and transferable.
points: Live modelling is most valuable when students are new to both the content and the process structure: chunking the model into explicit sequential stages allows students to focus on one component at a time and understand why each stage prepares the ground for the next.

Mid-model adaptation is not a failure of planning but a diagnostic practice: when check-for-understanding reveals a prior knowledge gap, the teacher must step away from the live model, re-teach the missing knowledge, and then return—proceeding without doing so undermines everything that follows.

When students have secure knowledge, skipping the upfront model and releasing them to independent work before revealing an exemplar generates learning through the gap between their attempt and the ideal—more productive than seeing the model before trying.

Live modelling in practice demonstrates how the six core teaching purposes interact: checking for understanding mid-model, focusing attention on a specific confused point, and accessing memory are all simultaneously active—purpose-switching happens in short bursts, not discrete phases.

The decision to use, adapt, or withhold live modelling must be calibrated to the learners' current state, not to subject or task type; the underlying principle is that teaching serves learning, and the technique must flex when the learner's needs diverge from the plan.
quotes: Live modelling refers to the teacher building up a model or example piece by piece in the moment, narrating their thought process as they go. Some teachers do this on a board or flip chart while others model onto paper under a visualiser so that the model is projected onto the board for students to see.

By chunking the model into these three component stages, students get to focus on one stage at a time, understanding how it prepares the ground for the next stage of the process and how each stage builds on the previous one.

When we pick up on the fact that students are not following our live model, an adaptation to the planned technique is necessary. Noureddine describes this as being about focusing student attention on the specific part of the model that has caused the confusion—the point in the process where understanding was lost.

Continuing with the pre-planned live modelling process would not be in the best interests of learning because students' misunderstanding of the word would have undermined their understanding of the interpretation of the quote that the teacher was modelling. When there is crucial knowledge that students need to have in place in order to access new learning, teachers need to make sure that that knowledge is in place before continuing, even if this means adapting away from a pre-planned technique.

This approach to live modelling might be well suited to a situation in which students are new to a text or to the convention of annotating quotations. The unfamiliar nature of the content or the task means that learning is well served by explicitly modelling the process so that the steps are replicable and logical.

When students know the content well and are familiar with the process, teachers might decide to ask them to complete the activity independently or in groups first before then comparing their work to a completed exemplar.
